experiments.title: How steep is too steep? The rubber-band ramp test
experiments.context: In this experiment you pull a loaded toy up a 10-centimetre step three ways. You go straight up, up a short ramp and up a long ramp. A rubber band shows how hard you pull. You find out why a long ramp is easier than a short one, and how much room a proper wheelchair ramp needs.
experiments.problem: A step stops wheels. A ramp lets wheels roll up, but only if it is gentle enough. In this test a rubber band measures the pull. The more the band stretches, the harder you are pulling.
experiments.question: Which way up a 10-centimetre step needs the smallest pull: straight up, a short ramp or a long ramp?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which way will stretch the rubber band the most, and which the least? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Every try uses the same toy, the same load, the same rubber band and the same 10-centimetre step. Only the way up changes. You pull slowly, taking about 5 seconds to reach the top. You do each way 3 times, because one try can be a fluke, and you use the middle number of the three.
results_table: My guess: most, middle or least stretch
Extra length over the resting band (cm)

materials.item: a toy lorry or car on wheels, with a flat place to carry a load
a load of half a kilogram, such as a packet of dal or sugar, taped onto the toy
a strong rubber band, about 5 millimetres wide, or two thin bands side by side
a thread about 40 centimetres long
books to build a step exactly 10 centimetres high
a 30-centimetre ruler
a board, tray or flattened cardboard carton about 100 centimetres long, for the long ramp
a short board or a thick hardcover book about 30 centimetres long, for the short ramp
a measuring tape or a piece of string, to mark 120 centimetres on the floor
a pencil and paper for the table

experiments.record: Write the band's resting length at the top of the table. Fill in the table for each way up. Then draw the three ways up, side by side, and write the extra length under each.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one family in Kochi
cols: Extra length over the resting band (cm)

setup.art: A stack of books exactly 10 centimetres high, with a ruler standing beside it, and a toy lorry loaded with a packet of dal on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Build a step 10 centimetres high. Load the toy.

setup.art: A thread tied to the front of the toy and to a rubber band, with a hand holding the band and a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Tie the thread to the toy and the band to the thread.

setup.art: Three pictures side by side: the toy lifted straight up the step, pulled up a short steep ramp and pulled up a long gentle ramp.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the toy up the step three ways.

setup.art: A 120-centimetre line of tape on the floor running away from the foot of the step.
setup.caption: 4. Mark out 120 centimetres, the length a proper ramp needs.

flow.do: Stack books until the step is exactly 10 centimetres high. Measure it with the ruler. Tape the load onto the toy. Tie the thread to the front of the toy, and tie the other end of the thread to the rubber band.
flow.say: Wheels cannot roll up a step. A wheelchair meets steps like this at doorways. Today we find out how much a ramp helps. This rubber band tells us how hard we pull. The more the band stretches, the harder the pull.
flow.kid: Build the step. Load the toy. Tie the thread to the toy and to the band.
flow.parent: Measure the band's resting length with the ruler and write it at the top of the table. Keep the thread short, about 20 centimetres, so the band pulls along the ramp. Test the load first. Hang the toy and its load from the band. If the band stretches to more than three times its resting length, use a lighter load. If it stretches by less than 3 centimetres, use a heavier load. Your numbers will differ from the example because every band and every toy is different. The order of the three ways is what matters.

flow.do: Show your child the three ways up: straight up, the short ramp and the long ramp. Ask for a guess about which stretches the band most and least, and why. Write the guess in the table.
flow.say: Which way will make the band stretch the most? Which the least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which way stretches the band most and which least. Say why you think so.
flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Write down the reason as well as the guess. The test will answer it, and you do not need to say who was right.

ask.q: Which way will stretch the band the most? Why?
good: Straight up, because I lift all of it.
The short ramp, because it is steep.
The long ramp, because I go further.

flow.do: Hold the ruler beside the band. Your child pulls the toy straight up from the floor to the top of the step, slowly, taking about 5 seconds. Read the band's length while the toy moves. Do this 3 times and write each number in the table.
flow.say: Lift the toy straight up, slowly. I will read the band while you lift.
flow.kid: Lift the toy straight up the step with the band. Go slowly. Your grown-up reads the ruler.
flow.parent: Read the number when the toy is halfway up, while it is moving steadily. If the toy swings, shorten the thread. Pull in a straight line along the slope and not sideways, so that the band shows only the pull.

flow.do: Rest the short board from the floor to the top of the step. Pull the toy up it by the band, slowly, three times, reading the ruler each time. Then do the same with the long board.
flow.say: Now the short ramp, then the long ramp. Same toy, same load, same band, same step. Only the way up changes.
flow.kid: Pull the toy up the short ramp three times. Then pull it up the long ramp three times.
flow.parent: Hold the lower end of each board so that it does not slide. A carton can sag, so lay a magazine under the middle of it. If the toy does not roll easily, use a different toy. A toy that drags on its wheels hides the result, because friction, the rubbing grip, pulls against you.

flow.do: Write the middle number of each way in the table. Take away the resting length to find the extra length. Put the three ways in order from the biggest extra length to the smallest. Compare with the guess.
flow.say: Which way stretched the band most? Which least? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Find the middle number for each way. Which way stretched the band most, and which least?

ask.q: Why did the long ramp need the smallest pull?
good: The toy goes up a little at a time.
The ramp holds up most of the weight.
You go further but each part is easy.

check.q: Which way up needed the smallest pull?
check.why: The long ramp rises only a little over each centimetre along. The ramp holds up most of the weight, so the pull is small. The price is a longer path.

flow.do: Lay a measuring tape or a string 120 centimetres long on the floor, starting at the foot of the step. Stand at the far end. Look back at the step.
flow.say: A real ramp may rise only 1 centimetre for every 12 along. Our step is 10 centimetres high. So the ramp must be 120 centimetres long. That is more than a whole arm span. Is that more room than you thought?
flow.kid: Look along the 120-centimetre line. That is how long a ramp for this step must be.
flow.parent: The test cannot show how tired a person's arms get, how a wet surface grips or how a ramp feels in rain. It also cannot show where a rest place is needed. Wheels, surface and arm strength all matter on a real ramp. The test does show one thing clearly: a longer slope needs a smaller push, and you pay for it with a longer path.
flow.think: What does this test not tell us about a real ramp for a wheelchair? What else would you test?

experiments.title: Wet or dry, smooth or rough: which surface stops a chappal slipping?
experiments.context: In this experiment you tilt a tray with a rubber chappal on it until the chappal starts to slide. You try a smooth dry tray, a smooth wet tray and a rough towel. You find out why a good ramp, and a bathroom floor, needs a rough surface.
experiments.problem: A steep and wet ramp can be dangerous for an old person with a stick, a child or anyone with wet feet. This test shows which surfaces grip best.
experiments.question: How high must we lift the tray before the chappal slides: on a smooth dry tray, a smooth wet tray and a rough towel?
experiments.predict: Guess first. On which surface will the chappal slide at the lowest tilt? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The tray, the chappal and the way you lift stay the same. You lift the end slowly, about one finger-width every 2 seconds, and the chappal starts at the same place each time. Only the surface changes. You do each surface 3 times, because one try can be a fluke, and you use the middle number.
results_table: My guess: slides first, second or last

materials.item: a smooth plastic tray or chopping board about 40 centimetres long
an old rubber chappal
a piece of rough towel or a coir doormat, big enough to cover the tray
a cup of water
a dry cloth for wiping
a 30-centimetre ruler
an old towel to put under the tray
a pencil and paper for the table

experiments.safety: Water on the floor can make anyone slip. Keep the tray over the old towel and wipe up any spills at once.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Write 'did not slip' if the chappal stays still when the end is lifted 30 centimetres. Draw the three surfaces and put them in order from slides first to slides last.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one family in Madurai

setup.art: A smooth plastic tray on an old towel on the floor, with one end against a wall and a rubber chappal sitting on it.
setup.caption: 1. Rest the tray with one end against a wall. Put the chappal in the middle.

setup.art: A child lifting the free end of the tray slowly, while a parent holds a ruler beside it and the chappal starts to slide.
setup.caption: 2. Lift the end slowly. Say 'stop' when the chappal slides. Measure the height.

setup.art: The same tray, now wet, and then covered by a rough towel, with the chappal on each.
setup.caption: 3. Repeat on the wet tray and on the rough towel.

flow.do: Lay the old towel on the floor. Rest the tray on it with one short end against a wall or a heavy bag so that it cannot slide away. Put the chappal in the middle of the tray, with its sole down.
flow.say: We will tilt the tray slowly. The chappal will slide when the tilt is steep enough. We will measure how high the free end is at that moment.
flow.kid: Rest the tray with one end against a wall. Put the chappal in the middle.
flow.parent: Check the ruler reads from the floor to the underside of the lifted end. Practice once. If the chappal slides while you set up, move it to the middle again.

flow.do: Ask for a guess about which surface the chappal slides on at the lowest tilt, and why. Write the guess in the table.
flow.say: Where will the chappal slide first: on the smooth dry tray, the wet tray or the rough towel? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess where the chappal slides first. Say why you think so.
flow.parent: Write the guess and the reason. Do not tell the answer. The test will show it.

ask.q: Where will the chappal slide first? Why?
good: The wet tray, because water makes it slippery.
The dry tray, because plastic is smooth.
The towel, because it is soft.

flow.do: On the smooth dry tray, your child lifts the free end slowly and says 'stop' when the chappal starts to slide. You hold the ruler beside the lifted end and read the height. Do this 3 times. Write each height in the table.
flow.say: Lift slowly, one finger-width every 2 seconds. Say 'stop' when the chappal starts to slide.
flow.kid: Lift the end slowly. Say 'stop' when the chappal slides. Your grown-up reads the height.
flow.parent: Put the chappal back in the middle each time. If the chappal does not slide by 30 centimetres, write 'did not slip' and stop lifting.

flow.do: Pour a spoonful of water on the tray and spread it with your hand so the tray is wet all over. Wet the chappal's sole too. Do the same lifting 3 times and write each height.
flow.say: Now the tray is wet. Will the chappal slide at a lower tilt or a higher tilt?
flow.kid: Wet the tray and the chappal. Lift slowly three times. Say 'stop' when it slides.
flow.parent: If the wet and dry heights are within 2 centimetres of each other, wet the sole more. Wipe up spills at once, because a wet floor can make anyone slip. Dry the tray and the chappal before the next step.

flow.do: Lay the rough towel flat on the dry tray. Put the chappal on it and lift 3 times. Write each height, or 'did not slip'.
flow.say: Now a rough towel. Will it grip better than the smooth tray, or worse?
flow.kid: Put the rough towel on the tray. Lift the end slowly three times.
flow.parent: If the towel bunches, tape its edges flat or hold it down at the corners with books.

flow.do: Find the middle number for each surface. Put the surfaces in order from slides first to slides last.
flow.say: Which surface lets the chappal slide first? Where would you want to walk on a rainy day, or with a stick?
flow.kid: Which surface slid first? Which gripped best?

check.q: Which surface is best for a ramp on a rainy day?
check.why: A rough surface grips shoes, sticks and wheels even when it is wet. A smooth wet surface lets them slide.

flow.think: Why do bathrooms and ramps need a rough surface? Where have you seen a rough mat on the floor?

activities.title: Steps and ramps near us: a survey of a door, a school or a shop
activities.context: In this activity you count the steps and look for ramps at your home, your school or a nearby shop. You measure one ramp and find out if it is gentle enough for a wheelchair. You find out who can get in easily and who cannot.
activities.problem: A building with only steps shuts out people who use wheelchairs, and also people with prams, trolleys and sticks. A ramp opens the way, but only if it is long enough.

materials.item: a measuring tape or a piece of string and a ruler
a pencil and paper for the table
a grown-up to walk with you

activities.safety: Stay with a grown-up near the road. Look at the ramp and the steps, and do not climb on rails.
activities.record: A table with one row for each place. Write the number of steps, whether there is a ramp, and whether there is a handrail.

setup.art: A child counting three steps at a shop door while a parent holds a measuring tape.
setup.caption: 1. Count the steps at a door and measure how high they rise.

setup.art: A long gentle ramp beside the steps, with a child measuring its length along the ground with string.
setup.caption: 2. Find a ramp. Measure how high it rises and how long it is.

flow.do: Walk to the main door of your building, your school or a nearby shop. Count the steps. Measure how high the steps rise in all.
flow.say: Look at the door. Could someone with a pram or a wheelchair get in without help? What is in the way?
flow.kid: Count the steps. Measure how high they go up.
flow.parent: A usual doorstep rises 10 to 20 centimetres. Measure from the ground to the top of the last step. If the place has no steps, notice that and write 'no steps'.

ask.q: Who could not get in easily?
good: An old person with a stick.

flow.do: Find a ramp, at your building or somewhere on the way. Measure how high it rises and how long it is along the ground. Divide the length by the height. If the answer is 12 or more, the ramp is gentle enough.
flow.say: Length divided by height. A ramp that goes up 15 centimetres over 180 centimetres gives 12. Is your ramp 12 or more? Does it have a handrail and a rough surface?
flow.kid: Measure how high the ramp goes up and how long it is. Is the long number at least 12 times the short number?
flow.parent: If you cannot find a ramp, measure a kerb slope on the pavement or a ramp in a mall or a station. Do the sum together: for a rise of 10 centimetres, a gentle ramp is at least 120 centimetres long. Many ramps in India are much steeper than 1 in 12, so it is a common finding.

flow.do: Draw the door, the steps and the ramp. Write where the ramp starts, the front or the back of the building, and whether a person could use it alone.
flow.say: Is the ramp at the front door, where everyone goes in, or round the back? What does that say to the person who uses it?
flow.kid: Draw the door, the steps and the ramp. Is the ramp at the front or the back?
flow.parent: Notice where the ramp is. A ramp tucked away beside the dustbins tells a person that she was not expected at the front door.
flow.think: Who is the building made for? What would you change first?

activities.title: Write your name in Braille with dal grains
activities.context: In this activity you glue dal grains onto card to make the raised dots of Braille. You write your name and then read it with your fingertips. You find out how six dots can make every letter, and why fingers can read.
activities.problem: A blind person reads with the fingertips. Braille uses six dots in two columns of three. Different patterns of dots stand for different letters.

materials.item: a piece of thick card, about the size of a postcard, from a cereal box or an old file cover
whole green gram (moong) dal or another small round dal, about 20 grains
white glue, such as Fevicol
a pencil and a ruler
a plate, to catch spilled grains

activities.record: Your name in dots on the card, and a drawing of the first letter's dot pattern on paper.

setup.art: A card with a grid of six pencil circles, three down the left and three down the right, numbered 1, 2, 3 on the left and 4, 5, 6 on the right.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the six-dot cell for each letter, 2 centimetres apart.

setup.art: A fingertip reading dal grains stuck in dot patterns on a card.
setup.caption: 2. Glue a grain on each dot you need. Let the glue dry. Then read with your fingertips.

flow.do: Draw a six-dot cell for each letter of your name, with the dots 2 centimetres apart. Number them: 1, 2, 3 down the left side, and 4, 5, 6 down the right side. Use the chart in the notes to find which dots each letter needs.
flow.say: Braille is made from a block of six dots. Each letter uses some of the six. The dot numbers go down the left side, then down the right side. Which dots do you need for the first letter of your name?
flow.kid: Draw the six dots for each letter of your name. Number them 1, 2, 3 down the left. Then number 4, 5, 6 down the right.
flow.parent: The dot chart. A is 1. B is 1 and 2. C is 1 and 4. D is 1, 4 and 5. E is 1 and 5. F is 1, 2 and 4. G is 1, 2, 4 and 5. H is 1, 2 and 5. I is 2 and 4. J is 2, 4 and 5. For K to T, take the letters A to J and add dot 3. For U, V, X, Y and Z, take A, B, C, D and E and add dots 3 and 6. W is a special one: 2, 4, 5 and 6. A name of three or four letters is enough. Real Braille cells are much smaller than these, smaller than a fingertip.

flow.do: Put a small dot of glue on each place where the chart says a dot is needed. Press one grain of dal into each glue dot. Leave the other dot places empty.
flow.say: A grain on each dot we need, and an empty place where there is no dot. Press each grain down gently.
flow.kid: Put a dot of glue where a dot is needed. Press a grain into it.
flow.parent: Use only a small dot of glue, as a big blob takes a long time to dry. If you do not have glue, use a small piece of sticky tape rolled into a ring.

flow.do: Leave the card to dry for 20 minutes. In that time, look for Braille at home, such as on a medicine box, a lift button or an identity card.
flow.say: While the glue dries, can you find Braille at home? Run a finger over a medicine box.
flow.kid: Look for Braille on a medicine box or a lift button.
flow.parent: Many medicine boxes carry the name in Braille. Some lift buttons and some ATM keys do. If you cannot find any, feel the raised marks near the edge of a clean note of 100, 200 or 500 rupees. These are for touch.

flow.do: Once the glue is dry, close your eyes so that only the fingers read. Run one fingertip lightly over each cell and say how many dots you feel. Then ask a friend or a grown-up to read your name with the chart.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Slide one fingertip over a cell. How many dots do you feel, and where? A blind reader does this fast, with practice. It takes months to learn.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Slide a fingertip over each cell. Count the dots.

ask.q: What was hard? What would help?
good: The dots felt too big or too small.
I forgot which cell was first.

flow.think: A person who reads Braille reads many words a minute. Why could fingers learn this?

activities.title: Ask, wait, do: practising how to offer help
activities.context: In this activity you practise what to say when you want to help someone. A grown-up reads a short scene aloud and answers as the person in it. You practise asking first, waiting, and accepting a 'no'.
activities.problem: Help can go wrong when the helper does not ask. In this activity you practise asking, waiting for the answer and doing what the person says. Nobody acts out a disability, because that is not how to learn about it. You only practise the words.

materials.item: the scenes below, read aloud by a grown-up

activities.record: Tick which scene each answer was: yes, no, or yes but a different way.

setup.art: A girl standing and asking a woman with two bags a question, with a speech bubble 'Would you like some help?'
setup.caption: 1. Ask first, face to face.

setup.art: The woman answering 'No, thank you' and the girl stepping back, with a speech bubble 'All right.'
setup.caption: 2. If the answer is no, say 'all right' and mean it.

flow.do: Tell your child the three steps: ask, wait, do what the person says. Say them together.
flow.say: When you want to help, there are three steps. Ask: 'Would you like some help?' Wait for the answer. Do what the person says. If the answer is no, say 'all right'.
flow.kid: Say the three steps: ask, wait, do what the person says.
flow.parent: Keep the scenes about words only. Nobody pretends to have a disability. You read each scene aloud, then answer in your own voice as the person in it.

flow.do: Read the scenes one at a time. Your child says what to say and do first. Then you answer as the person. Scene 1 is a woman at a shop door with two heavy bags. You say yes. Scene 2 is an old neighbour on the stairs, who has a stick. You say no thank you. Scene 3 is a person in a wheelchair at a door. You say, 'Please hold the door.' You go through yourself. Scene 4 is a blind woman at a bus stop. You say, 'Please let me hold your elbow.' Scene 5 is a deaf girl at the next desk. You write, 'No thank you, I am fine.'
flow.say: Here is the first scene. A woman at a shop door has two heavy bags. What do you say?
flow.kid: Listen to each scene. Say what you say first. Then do what the person says.
flow.parent: Praise asking and waiting, more than doing. In scene 2, the child should say 'All right' and stop. In scene 3, the child holds the door and does not touch the chair. In scene 4, offer an elbow, and walk at the person's pace. In scene 5, stand where she can see your face and write or speak normally. Do not talk over the person's head to a friend.

flow.do: Ask your child to tell one time when someone helped without asking, and how it felt. Then ask what could be done instead.
flow.say: Has someone ever 'helped' you without asking? How did it feel? What could they have said?
flow.kid: Think of a time someone helped without asking. How did it feel?
flow.think: What would you like a helper to say to you first?

activities.title: Hands full: three jobs and a better design
activities.context: In this activity you do three everyday jobs while your arms are busy carrying things. You find out which handle, switch or cap works best, and you draw a change that would help everyone. You find out that good design helps people with full hands, small hands and weak hands.
activities.problem: Sometimes a door, a tap or a bottle is hard to use because the object was made for hands that are free. A better design works for many hands, not only for some.

materials.item: a school bag or a big bag of shopping
a steel tumbler with water in it
a door or cupboard with a handle
a bottle with a screw cap
a sheet of paper and colours

activities.record: A drawing of one object with your change marked on it.

setup.art: A child with a school bag on one arm and a tumbler of water in the other hand, using an elbow to push down a lever door handle.
setup.caption: 1. Carry a bag and a tumbler. Try three jobs.

setup.art: A drawing of a round door knob beside a long lever handle, with an arrow to the lever and a smile.
setup.caption: 2. Compare the handles. Draw your change.

flow.do: Put the school bag on one arm and hold the tumbler of water in the other hand. Try three jobs: open a door that has a handle, press a switch, and unscrew a bottle cap. Notice which job was easiest and which was hardest.
flow.say: Your hands are busy. Try three jobs. Which was the easiest, and which was hardest? What would have helped?
flow.kid: Carry a bag and a tumbler. Open a door, press a switch and open a bottle. Which was hardest?
flow.parent: This is about objects and not about disability. It shows how an object can fail anyone whose hands are busy. A person who lives with a disability is the real expert on what works, so ask people and listen. Keep the tumbler only half full so that nothing spills.

good: The door with a lever handle, because I used my elbow.
The switch, because I pressed it with my knuckle.

flow.do: Look at the door handle again. Is it a round knob, a pull handle or a long lever? Try it with your elbow. Which type works best when your hands are busy?
flow.say: A long handle can be pushed with an elbow. A round knob needs a hand that can grip and turn. Which works for more people?
flow.kid: Try the handle with your elbow. Which kind of handle works for the most people?
flow.parent: Lever handles were made for hands that cannot grip a round knob. They also help anyone with full arms, a small child, or someone with wet hands.

flow.do: Your child draws one object with a change to make it easier for many hands. Label who it helps.
flow.say: Draw the change you would make. Who would it help?
flow.kid: Draw a change to make one object easier. Write who it helps.
flow.think: If a design works for the hands that find it hardest, will it also work for everyone else?

activities.title: Ask an elder: what they know and what would make their day easier
activities.context: In this activity you talk with an older person and write down what they tell you. Then you look at one place at home that might trip an older person. You find out that old people hold what families know, and that small changes keep them safe.
activities.problem: Old age changes eyes, ears, bones and balance, and old people carry stories, songs, recipes and cures. This activity listens to one elder and checks one path at home for safety.

materials.item: an older person, such as a grandparent, a neighbour, a relative or a teacher. If there is none near you, phone one or ask a grown-up to introduce you
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Three things the elder told you, and one change that would make their day easier.

setup.art: A child and an old woman sitting side by side, the child writing in a notebook while the woman talks and gestures.
setup.caption: 1. Ask the elder three questions. Write the answers.

setup.art: A hallway with a night light, a rough mat and a handrail, with a child pointing to each.
setup.caption: 2. Check one path at home for light, a dry floor and a non-slip mat.

flow.do: Sit beside an older person, face to face, in a quiet place. Ask three questions: What did you play when you were small? What is one thing you can cook that nobody writes down? What would make your day easier? Write the answers.
flow.say: Look at the person, speak a little slower and wait for the answer. Shouting does not help, because it bends the sounds.
flow.kid: Ask the elder three questions. Write what they say.
flow.parent: Choose a time when the elder is rested and not hurried. If the person has trouble hearing, sit where your face is in the light. Let the elder finish the story, even if it is long. If the elder chooses not to answer a question, say 'all right'.

flow.do: Walk the path an older person uses at home, from the bed to the bathroom. Check three things: is there light, is the floor dry, and is there a non-slip mat where the floor gets wet?
flow.say: Walk the path as an older person would. Is it well lit? Is the floor dry? Is there a rough mat in the bathroom?
flow.kid: Check the path from the bed to the bathroom. Is there light? Is the floor dry? Is there a rough mat?
flow.parent: A light left on at night, a rough mat and a handrail prevent many falls. Ask the older person what they would change. They are the expert.

flow.do: Your child tells the elder or the family one thing learned and one thing that could change at home.
flow.say: What did the elder tell you? What is one change we can make?
flow.kid: Tell your family one thing the elder said and one change you could make.
flow.think: What would we lose if nobody asked the oldest people what they know?

activities.title: A get-well card and soap-and-water hands
activities.context: In this activity you plan how to care for someone who is ill, make a get-well card, and practise washing your hands with soap. You find out what a sick person needs, and how to care without spreading the illness.
activities.problem: A sick person needs rest, water, light food and company. A carer needs to keep germs from spreading, so hands are washed with soap after helping.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and colours
soap and a tap
a clock or a watch with a seconds hand

activities.record: A get-well card with a drawing and two kind sentences.

setup.art: A child drawing a get-well card at a table, with a list headed 'Rest, water, food, company'.
setup.caption: 1. List what a sick person needs, then make a card.

setup.art: Two hands covered in soap bubbles under a tap, with a clock showing 20 seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds.

flow.do: Think of someone you know who is ill, or has been ill. List four things a sick person needs. Ask: what could a child do?
flow.say: A sick person needs rest, water, light food and company. Who do you know who is unwell? What could you do for them?
flow.kid: List what a sick person needs. Think of one thing you can do.
flow.parent: Keep this about care and company, and not about fear. If your child knows someone with a serious illness, listen first.

ask.q: What does a sick person need?

flow.do: Make a get-well card. Draw a picture and write two kind sentences in big, clear letters. The card can be given in person, sent in a message or read out over the phone.
flow.say: Write two kind sentences in big letters. A sick person can read a clear card even when tired.
flow.kid: Draw a card and write two kind sentences in big, clear letters.
flow.parent: A card, a drawing or a phone call reaches someone when a visit is not allowed. Ask your child to ask the sick person what they would like, rather than guess.

flow.do: Wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds. Count slowly or sing a song twice. Rub the backs of the hands, between the fingers and the thumbs.
flow.say: After you help a sick person, wash with soap for 20 seconds. Soap and water wash germs away so they do not pass on to others.
flow.kid: Wash your hands with soap. Count to 20. Wash the backs of your hands and between your fingers.
flow.parent: Wash your own hands before and after you help, and keep a cloth ready for the sick person's cough.

flow.do: Send or give the card, or put it where you will remember to give it.
flow.say: When will you give the card? How will the sick person feel when it comes?
flow.kid: Give or send your card.
flow.think: Is a card enough, or is company better? What does a sick person like best?

activities.title: Watch one animal for five minutes: what does she need?
activities.context: In this activity you watch one animal from a distance for five minutes. The animal can be a crow, a squirrel, a pigeon, a street dog or a cow. You notice what she is doing and what she might need. You find out how animals tell us what they need without words.
activities.problem: Animals feel thirst, hunger, heat and fear. They tell us with their bodies. A dog who turns away and tucks her tail says 'keep away'. This activity practises noticing.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a watch or a clock
a window, a balcony or a quiet spot where you can watch from a distance

activities.safety: Watch from a distance of at least three big steps, with a grown-up beside you. Do not touch, feed or chase an animal you do not know.
activities.record: A table: what the animal did, and what she might need.

setup.art: A child sitting at a window with a notebook, watching a crow on a wall.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one animal. Watch for five minutes.

setup.art: A notebook page with two columns, 'What she did' and 'What she might need', and a few drawings.
setup.caption: 2. Write what she did and what she might need.

flow.do: Choose one animal you can see from a distance. Watch her for five minutes without making any noise. Write each thing she does.
flow.say: Watch one animal for five minutes. What does she do? Where does she go?
flow.kid: Watch one animal for five minutes. Write each thing she does.
flow.parent: Choose a crow, a pigeon, a squirrel, a dog, a cow or any animal near you. If you see a street dog, keep your distance and watch her body for signs that she wants to be left alone.

flow.do: Look at your notes. For each action, write what she might need: water, shade, food, safety or to be left alone.
flow.say: What might she need? Is she thirsty, hot, hungry or afraid? How can you tell?
flow.kid: For each thing she did, write what she might need.

flow.do: Talk about one thing you could do to help her, and one thing you must not do.
flow.say: What is one kind thing you could do? What is one thing we must not do, such as chasing or teasing?
flow.kid: Say one kind thing to do and one thing not to do.
flow.think: How can you know what an animal needs when she cannot tell you in words?

games.title: Fix It Together: barrier cards
games.context: This is a card game about places that shut some people out. Each card shows a barrier. You say one way to fix it and who else the fix helps. Then you turn the card over to see a fix. You find out that a change made for some people often helps many.

items.f: A school has three steps at the gate and no ramp.
items.b: Fix: a ramp at the main gate with a handrail. Also helps: a parent with a pram, a child with a heavy bag, a teacher with a broken ankle.

items.f: A bus has a high first step and nothing to hold.
items.b: Fix: a low step or a ramp, and a handrail. Also helps: old people, a mother with a baby, small children.

items.f: A bus stop board shows the names of places only in small written letters.
items.b: Fix: big clear letters and a voice that calls out each stop. Also helps: a person who cannot see the board, a visitor who cannot read the language, a child still learning to read.

items.f: A railway platform edge looks the same as the rest of the platform.
items.b: Fix: yellow bumpy tiles along the edge. Also helps: a child running, a person looking at a phone, anyone in a hurry.

items.f: A video has speech but no words on the screen.
items.b: Fix: show the words at the bottom of the screen. Also helps: a person who cannot hear, people on a noisy bus, a person learning the language.

items.f: A shop door has a round knob and is very heavy.
items.b: Fix: a long lever handle and a door that swings easily. Also helps: a person with full hands, a small child, a person with a weak grip.

items.f: A bathroom floor is smooth tile and often wet.
items.b: Fix: a rough non-slip mat and a handrail on the wall. Also helps: old people, small children, anyone with wet feet.

items.f: A clinic calls out names loudly, and people wait in a crowd.
items.b: Fix: also show each number on a screen and call it clearly. Also helps: a person who cannot hear, a person at the back, a person who does not know the language.

items.f: A lift has flat buttons with no marks.
items.b: Fix: raised numbers and Braille beside each button. Also helps: a person pressing the button in the dark, a person who cannot see, anyone carrying a lot.

items.f: A doorway is narrow, and a wheelchair cannot turn through it.
items.b: Fix: widen the door so a wheelchair can pass and turn. Also helps: a person carrying a big box, two people walking together, a trolley.

items.f: A class only lets pupils show answers by speaking aloud in front of all.
items.b: Fix: let pupils also write, draw or show the answer. Also helps: a shy child, a child still learning the language, a child who speaks slowly.

items.f: A playground game needs everyone to run fast across a field.
items.b: Fix: change a rule so that all can join, such as passing a ball instead of running, or each player choosing the distance. Also helps: a younger child, a tired runner, a child with a sore foot.

rules: Cut out the 12 barrier cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top card and read the front aloud.
Say one way to fix the barrier, and name one person the fix would help.
Now read the back. If your fix matches the back, or is another good fix, you get 1 point.
If you named a helper that is on the back, or another real person who would be helped, you get 1 more point.
Put the card at the bottom of the pile. When every card has been turned once, count the points. The player with the most points wins. If the points are equal, both win.
To play alone, try to score 18 points out of 24, and play again to beat your score. To play with friends, score as a team and try to beat your last score.

setup.art: Twelve barrier cards face down in a pile on a table, and a child reading the top card aloud.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the cards and put them face down.

setup.art: A child pointing to the back of a card that shows a ramp, and a parent counting points on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Say a fix, turn the card, and count your points.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Mix them and put them face down in a pile. Explain the scoring: 1 point for a fix, 1 more point for naming who else it helps.
flow.say: Each card shows a barrier. You say a fix. A fix that helps many people is worth more.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them. Put them face down.

flow.do: Take turns. Turn over a card and read it aloud. Say a fix and a helper. Then read the back and count points. Talk about any card where you disagree.
flow.say: What would you change? Who else does it help? Is there a second good fix?
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Say a fix and who it helps. Check the back.
flow.parent: Many cards have more than one good fix. If your child gives a different fix that works, give the point. Help your child think about who is shut out and who else benefits.

ask.q: Is there a second good fix?
good: Yes, a different fix also works.
The back gives one idea, but others are fine.

flow.do: Count the points. Ask which card surprised your child most.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Which fix helps the most people?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card surprised you?

games.title: Helper Pairs: a matching game
games.context: This is a memory game with 16 cards. Eight cards name a helper, such as Braille or a ramp. Eight cards say what the helper does. You turn over two cards at a time to find the pairs. You find out what each helper does and who else it helps.

printables.title: 16 cards to cut out: 8 helpers and 8 jobs
items: Reads by touch, with raised dots
Sweeps ahead to find steps, poles and holes
Talks with the hands, face and body
Lets wheels roll up to a higher place
A foot that bends, so the wearer can squat and walk on rough ground
Bumpy tiles whose lines mean go on and dots mean stop
A bar to hold for a steady grip on a stair or a ramp

rules: Cut out the 16 cards. Mix them and lay them face down in four rows of four.
Take turns. Turn over two cards. If one names a helper and the other says what it does, they are a pair. Keep the pair.
If they are not a pair, turn them face down again in the same places.
When you make a pair, say one other person the helper could also help. If you can, you get 1 extra point.
Each pair is 1 point. When all the pairs are found, count your points. The player with the most points wins. If the points are equal, both win.
To play alone, count the turns it takes to find all 8 pairs, and try to do it in fewer turns next time.

setup.art: Sixteen cards face down in four rows of four on a table, and a child holding two cards turned face up.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the cards face down in four rows of four.

setup.art: Two matching cards, 'Ramp' and 'Lets wheels roll up to a higher place', side by side, with a child smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Turn two cards. Keep a pair if they match.

flow.do: Cut out the cards, mix them and lay them face down in four rows of four.
flow.say: Eight helpers and eight jobs. Match each helper to its job.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them. Lay them face down.

flow.do: Take turns to turn over two cards. Keep any pair. After each pair, say another person who could use the helper too.
flow.say: Is this a pair? Who else could use a ramp? Who else could use a handrail?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Keep a pair. Say who else could use it.

ask.q: Who else could use a ramp?
good: An old person with a stick.

flow.do: Count the pairs and the extra points. Ask which helper your child would like to learn more about.
flow.say: Which helper would you like to know more about?
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Which helper do you want to know more about?

projects.title: One small job for a week
projects.context: In this project you take over one small job at home for a week, and see how much time and care it takes. You find out that care work is real work. Sharing it is a way to care for the people who do it every day.

a pencil

flow.say: Who does these jobs? Which one will you take over for a week?
flow.kid: Ask who does each job. Choose one job to do for a week.
flow.parent: Any child can do any job. Choose a job that really helps the person who does it now, and is safe for your child. Do not choose a job with a knife, a stove or a hot pan.

flow.kid: Add up the minutes. Tell your family what you noticed.
flow.think: Who does the jobs that nobody sees? How could we share them?

challenges.title: A ramp for a step when there is not much room
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a ramp for a loaded toy lorry to climb a 10-centimetre step. A proper ramp must be 120 centimetres long, but you only have 70 centimetres of floor. You find out how to solve a real problem when space is short.
challenges.problem: A step is 10 centimetres high. The rule for a wheelchair ramp is a slope of 1 in 12, which is 1 centimetre up for every 12 along. That is 120 centimetres. But the space in front of the step is only 70 centimetres long. Build a model ramp so that the loaded toy lorry can climb with a small pull.
constraints: The ramp must rise no more than 1 centimetre for every 12 centimetres along.
You have only 70 centimetres of floor in a straight line.
It must have edges so the wheels do not roll off.
It must work with the loaded toy and the rubber band from the ramp test.

materials.item: books to build the 10-centimetre step
a flat piece of card or cardboard, a few sheets, cut into strips
sticky tape
a ruler
the toy lorry, the load and the rubber band from the ramp test
a grown-up to cut card

challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts the card. Stay clear of the cut edges.

setup.art: A stack of books as a step and 70 centimetres of floor marked with tape, with a long 120-centimetre line of tape curving round a corner.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the 70 centimetres of floor and the 10-centimetre step.

setup.art: A toy lorry going up a ramp that makes a turn at a flat landing, with low edges on each side.
setup.caption: 2. Build the ramp, test it with the toy and the band.

general: Use a straight ramp 120 centimetres long, and move the start of it to the side so that it runs along a wall.
Make the ramp longer and gentler, and rest it on a stack of books at the middle for support.
Use a rough surface, such as a strip of cloth taped on the card, so that wheels and feet grip.
creative: Build the ramp in two straight runs of 60 centimetres with a flat landing between them. The path turns round, so the ramp fits in a small space. Real ramps beside shops and railway stations use this.
Make the ramp fold up against the wall, so it is only out when someone needs it.
Build a ramp that runs round the corner of the step, with a gentle bend, so it uses the space beside the door.
challenges.your_turn: What is your own way to fit a long gentle ramp into a small space? Draw it and test it.

flow.do: Build the 10-centimetre step. Mark 70 centimetres of floor in front of it with tape. Read the problem aloud.
flow.say: A proper ramp for this step needs 120 centimetres. We have only 70 centimetres. What can we do?
flow.kid: Build the step. Mark 70 centimetres on the floor. Read the problem.

ask.q: What could you do when there is not enough room?
good: Move the ramp to another side.

flow.do: Your child plans a ramp on paper, then builds it from card, books and tape. Test it by pulling the loaded toy up with the rubber band. Measure how long the ramp is and how high it rises.
flow.say: Does the ramp rise no more than 1 centimetre for every 12? How does the band stretch?
flow.kid: Plan the ramp. Build it. Test it with the toy and the band.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the card. If the ramp is too steep, make it longer by adding a turn. Compare the band's stretch to the straight 100-centimetre ramp in the ramp test. A good answer has a small stretch. There is more than one good answer, and none is the only right one.

flow.do: Show your ramp to the family. Say what each part does and what you would change.
flow.say: Tell us how your ramp works. What would you change?
flow.kid: Show your ramp. Say what each part does.
flow.think: A turn makes the ramp longer. Why is that all right?

challenges.title: A sign that anyone can read, by sight or by touch
challenges.context: In this challenge you design a sign for a room at home or school, such as the kitchen. The sign must work for people who see well, people who see a little and people who cannot see.
challenges.problem: A small sign with thin letters is hard to read for someone who cannot see well. It cannot be read at all by a person who cannot see. Design a sign that can be read by sight and by touch.
constraints: The sign must have big letters in a dark colour on a pale background.
Part of the sign must be raised so that fingers can feel it.
It must be at a height that a hand can reach, about 1 metre from the floor.
It must be firm and fixed so it does not fall.

materials.item: a piece of thick card
a thick black marker pen
string, dal grains or thick paint for the raised part
white glue
sticky tape

setup.art: A piece of thick card with a big dark word 'KITCHEN', a raised string outline of a cup, and dots of dal below.
setup.caption: 1. Draw big dark letters. Add raised parts with string or grains.

setup.art: The sign fixed to a door at the height of a child's shoulder, with a hand reading the raised cup.
setup.caption: 2. Fix the sign on the door at hand height.

general: Draw big dark letters on a pale card, and glue a string outline of a picture, such as a cup for the kitchen.
Stick dal grains in a pattern next to the word, with the same pattern on every sign of the same kind.
Fix the sign on the door side where the handle is, at the height of a hand.
creative: Put a different rough mat in front of each door, so that feet can tell which room it is.
Use a different smell for each room, such as a small bag of tulsi leaves near the kitchen door.
Add a bell or a sound to a door that is often missed.
challenges.your_turn: How else can a person know which room it is, without looking? Add your own idea to the sign.

flow.do: Choose a room. Read the problem. Ask your child who needs to find this room and how they find it.
flow.say: How does a person know which room it is? Who may not be able to read a small sign?
flow.kid: Choose a room. Think about who needs the sign.

good: A visitor who has not been here before.
A person who cannot see well.

flow.do: Draw big dark letters on the card. Glue string or grains to make a raised picture or a raised pattern. Let it dry as far as you can, then tape the sign to a door.
flow.say: Big letters, a raised picture and the right height. What does each part do?
flow.kid: Draw big letters. Glue a raised picture. Tape the sign to the door.
flow.parent: Let the glue set for a few minutes, or use sticky tape to hold the grains until they dry. Ask a family member to try reading it by touch with eyes closed.

flow.do: Ask someone to read your sign by touch. Ask what they would change.
flow.say: Can you read it with your fingers? What would make it better?
flow.kid: Ask someone to read your sign by touch.
flow.think: Which part of the sign helps most people? Which part helps only a few?

items.p: A heavy load must go up a 10-centimetre step. Which way needs the smallest push?
items.why: A long ramp rises only a little over each centimetre along, so the ramp carries most of the weight. A short steep ramp needs a bigger pull, and a straight lift needs the biggest.

items.p: Everybody needs help at some time in life.
items.why: True. A baby needs help with everything, a person who is ill needs help, and most people need help in old age.

items.p: In the ramp test, the rubber band stretched ____ on the long ramp than on the short ramp.
items.why: The long ramp is gentler, so the pull is smaller and the band stretches less.

items.p: Draw a line from each helper to what it does.
pairs: Lets wheels roll up a step
items.why: Each helper is made for one job. Braille is read by touch, a cane sweeps the ground ahead, a hearing aid makes sound louder and a ramp replaces a step.
items.art: Four helpers on the left, Braille, a white cane, a hearing aid and a ramp, and four jobs on the right, with dots to join.

items.p: Put these in the order you do them when you want to help someone.
items: Do it the way the person says
a: Do it the way the person says
items.why: Ask first, then wait, then do what the person says. If the answer is no, say 'all right'.

items.p: Sort each helper by what it mainly does.
items.why: Braille and sign language carry words. A wheelchair, a Jaipur Foot and a white cane help a person move along.

items.p: You see a blind woman at a busy crossing. What do you do first?
opts: Hold her cane and lead her
items.why: Ask first, and do what she says. Holding the cane, or pulling her, takes charge of her body without her yes.

items.p: A friend says 'Poor thing, she cannot walk' about a girl in a wheelchair. What could your friend say instead?
items.a: A good answer says hello, or asks her name, or talks about what she likes. Or it says the step is the trouble, not her legs.
items.why: Pity looks down at a person. Asking and talking treats her as an equal.

items.p: Look at the school gate. Label one thing that helps a wheelchair user and one that stops her.
items.a: Helps: the long ramp with a handrail. Stops: the three steps.
items.why: A ramp opens the way. Steps close it.
items.art: A school gate with three steps on the left and a long ramp with a handrail on the right.

items.p: Draw a ramp for a doorstep. Show where it starts and ends. Write 'long' or 'short' beside it.
items.a: A drawing of a long, gentle slope up to the doorstep, labelled 'long'.
items.why: A long, gentle ramp needs a small push. A short ramp is steep and hard to climb.

items.p: A school wants a ramp. Two children talk about where to put it.

views.says: Put it at the front door. Then everyone goes in the same way.
Put it at the side door, where there is more room for a long gentle ramp, and make that a main door too.

items.ask: Which do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: Either side, with a reason. The first child is right that one way in for everyone says 'you belong here'. The second child is right that a ramp needs enough room to be gentle.
items.why: A strong answer weighs the room a long ramp needs against the message of the front door.

items.p: To be kind, a helper should always push a wheelchair without asking.
items.why: False. The chair is part of the user's own space. Ask first, and do what the person says.

items.p: A step is 10 centimetres high. A ramp must be 12 times as long. How many centimetres long is the ramp?
items.why: 10 x 12 = 120. The ramp must be at least 120 centimetres long.

items.p: A doorway is 20 centimetres above the road. What is the shortest ramp that fits the 1 in 12 rule?
items.why: 20 x 12 = 240. A ramp of 120 centimetres is right for a 10-centimetre step, and 40 centimetres is far too short.

items.p: A steep ramp squeezed into a small space always counts as help.
items.why: False. A steep ramp can be as useless as stairs for someone alone in a wheelchair. It must be gentle enough.

items.p: In the chappal test, on which surface did the chappal slide first?
items.why: Water on a smooth surface makes it slippery, so the chappal slid at the lowest tilt. The rough towel gripped best.

items.p: Match each person to a good first thing to do.
pairs: Face her in the light and speak normally, or write
Offer your elbow and let him hold it
Talk to her, not over her head
Do not pet or feed without asking the person
items.why: Each fits what the person needs. Faces help lip reading. An elbow lets the person guide. Talking to the person respects her. A guide dog in harness is working.

items.p: A ramp made for wheelchairs also helps a parent with a ____.
items.why: A pram, a trolley and a suitcase on wheels all roll up the same ramp. A change for some people helps many.

items.p: Indian Sign Language and American Sign Language are the same language.
items.why: False. Each country has its own sign languages, as it has its own spoken languages.

items.p: A girl who is blind says she has a full picture of her room. Could she be right? Say why.
items.a: Yes. She can know her room by touch, sound and echoes. The part of the brain for seeing is used for touch and hearing in people who are blind from early life. Every being builds its world from its own senses.
items.why: A strong answer says that a world made by touch and sound is full, and gives one reason.

items.p: Put these in order from the smallest push to the biggest push for a load going up a 10-centimetre step.
items.why: The longer the ramp, the smaller the push. Lifting straight up is like a ramp of no length, so it needs the biggest push.

items.p: Two people look at a woman in a wheelchair who cannot get into a shop with one step.

views.says: Her legs do not work, so the problem is in her body.

views.who: A woman who uses a wheelchair
views.says: A ramp would let me in, so the problem is the step.

items.ask: Which do you agree with? Why? Then say what the other has right.
items.a: Either side, with a reason. Both hold some truth: legs that do not walk are a difference, and a step is a barrier. People still argue about how much weight each gets.
items.why: A strong answer accepts that a body is different and that the world could be built another way.

items.p: Draw a good ramp. Label three things that make a ramp good.
items.a: A gentle slope, a handrail, a rough surface and a flat place to rest.
items.why: A good ramp is gentle, has a rail to hold, a surface that grips and a place to rest.

items.p: A rat opens a cage to free another rat, even with chocolate nearby. What does this suggest?
opts: Some animals help others who are trapped
items.why: In the test, many rats freed a trapped rat before eating the chocolate. This is one sign that animals other than humans help each other.

worksheets.title: Faulty ideas, fair tests and open questions (challenge)

items.p: A friend says, 'A ramp built for a wheelchair only helps wheelchair users.' What is the best reply?
opts: Prams, trolleys, suitcases and old people use it too
items.why: A ramp helps anyone with wheels or weak legs. This is why designing for the people with the most difficulty works for almost everyone.

items.p: A longer ramp for the same height needs a smaller push, but you push along a longer path.
items.why: True. You pay for the easier push with a longer way. Nothing comes free.

items.p: What can the rubber-band ramp test not tell us about a real wheelchair ramp?
items.a: It cannot show how tired a person's arms get, how a wet surface grips, where a rest place is needed, or how the ramp feels to use in rain.
items.why: A test answers one question. A real ramp has more to it: arms, surface, rest and weather.

items.p: A ramp is 300 centimetres long and rises 30 centimetres. Does it fit the 1 in 12 rule?
opts: Yes, any ramp fits the rule
No, it needs at least 360 centimetres
items.why: 30 x 12 = 360. A ramp of 300 centimetres is too steep by 60 centimetres. The wrong answer 'yes' only compares 300 with 30.

items.p: Should a deaf child get a cochlear implant? Three people see it differently.

views.who: An ear doctor and a mother
views.says: The child will hear and speak with the family, so say yes.
We are not broken. We have a language and a community. Do not change the child to fit others.
Give the implant and teach sign language too, so the child has two ways to talk.

items.ask: Which do you agree with, and why? What would you ask the child when she is older?
items.a: Any side, with a reason. There is no single right answer. Good answers ask what the child and her family value.
items.why: Deaf people and doctors still disagree. No view here is marked right.

items.p: We cannot feel another animal's pain, so nobody can tell if any animal feels pain.
items.why: False. We know another person's pain only from what they do and how their body is built. Scientists use the same evidence for animals.

items.p: Which is the best sign that a dog with a thorn in her paw feels pain?
opts: She guards the paw, licks it and whimpers when it is touched
items.why: Guarding a hurt part, licking it and pulling away are signs of pain. Dogs also have nerves like ours that carry signals of harm.

items.p: Someone says, 'Helping disabled people is a favour.' What do you think? Use the word 'right' in your answer.
items.a: A good answer says that people have a right to go to school and catch a bus, so a ramp is not a favour. Help comes with ask-first and respect.
items.why: India's law of 2016 says schools, offices, buses and websites must be usable. A right needs no thank you.

items.p: Sort each action by whether it respects the person.
items: Grabbing a bag to carry it
items.why: Asking and accepting a no keep the person in charge. Pushing, pulling and grabbing take charge without a yes.

items.p: A ramp must rise no more than 1 centimetre for every ____ centimetres along.
items.why: India's building guidelines give 1 in 12 as the steepest slope for a wheelchair ramp.

items.p: Look at the bird water dish. Label two things that make it safe and one thing that is wrong.
items.a: Safe: shade and a stone to stand on, fresh water. Wrong: a cat hiding behind the pot, or dirty water.
items.why: A good dish is shallow, in shade, has a stone, and is out of reach of cats. Old water can breed mosquitoes.
items.art: A clay dish of water on a wall in the shade with a stone in it, and a cat hiding behind a flowerpot.

items.p: Why is sharing care work a way to care for the carer?
opts: Care work is not real work
The carer gets time to rest
items.why: Care work is tiring, so a carer who gets help can rest. The jobs do not belong to one sex.

quiz.p: A girl broke her arm and cannot button her shirt for a month. What does this show?
opts: Anyone can need help for a while
She is not trying hard enough
quiz.why: Every person needs help at some time, as a baby, when hurt or ill, and often in old age. Needing help is part of life, not a rare thing.

quiz.p: A teacher says, 'We help them, and they are not like us.' What is the problem?
opts: Everybody needs help from others at some time
quiz.why: If everybody gets help at some time, 'them' and 'us' is not a true split. The helper today may need help tomorrow.

quiz.p: A load goes up a 10-centimetre step by a 120-centimetre ramp or a 30-centimetre ramp. Which needs the smaller push?
quiz.why: The long ramp rises only a little for each centimetre along, so the push is smaller. The price is a longer path.

quiz.p: A step is 15 centimetres high. How long must a ramp of slope 1 in 12 be at least?
quiz.why: 15 x 12 = 180. Adding 12 to 15 gives 27, and mixing up the numbers gives 90. For each 1 centimetre up, the ramp must go at least 12 along.

quiz.p: A blind person sweeps a white cane along the ground ahead of her. What is the cane for?
opts: To tell others to stay away
To find steps, poles and holes before her feet reach them
quiz.why: The cane gives her news of the ground ahead through touch. It is a tool for finding the way and does not warn others off.

quiz.p: Why was the Jaipur Foot built to bend and made of rubber?
opts: So that it looks like a shoe
So the wearer can squat and walk barefoot on rough ground
So it is heavy and strong
quiz.why: Many people in India sit on the floor, squat, and work barefoot in fields. A foot that bends and grips matches how they really live.

quiz.p: You offer help and the person says, 'No, thank you.' What do you do?
opts: Say 'all right' and let her do it herself
Ask a grown-up to make her accept
quiz.why: The person knows her own needs. Accepting a no keeps her in charge. Helping anyway takes charge of her.

quiz.p: Which sentence shows respect for a deaf boy?
opts: 'I will face him, and speak normally or write.'
quiz.why: Facing him lets him see your face and lips. 'Poor thing' is pity, and ignoring him leaves him out.

quiz.p: India's law of 2016 says schools, offices and buses must be usable by disabled people. What idea is behind it?
opts: Help is a favour from kind people
Help is a right that people are owed
quiz.why: A right needs no thank you. If a step is in the way, the step must go. Charity is good but it is not the same as a right.

quiz.p: An old man's balance is less sure now. Which helps him most at home?
opts: A light on at night and a mat that does not slip
quiz.why: Falls are a danger in old age, so light, a dry floor and a rough mat prevent them. A smooth floor and things moved around cause trips.

quiz.p: A friend is ill with a fever at home. Which is the best way to care?
opts: Bring water, sit with her, and wash your hands with soap after
Tell her to get up and run
Shout loudly so that she cannot sleep
quiz.why: A sick body needs rest, water, light food and company. Soap and water stop the germs passing to you or others.

quiz.p: A street dog turns away and tucks her tail when you come close. What is she telling you?
opts: I do not want you near me, so back away
quiz.why: Animals answer with the body. A dog who turns away or tucks her tail is saying no, just as a person might say 'No, thank you'.

quiz.p: On a hot day, which helps a thirsty sparrow most?
opts: Loud crackers to make her fly
A shallow dish of clean water in the shade
quiz.why: Animals feel thirst and heat. A shallow dish of water in the shade with a stone to stand on is real help. Crackers frighten, and plastic bags can harm.

quiz.p: A friend says, 'Only one child uses a wheelchair, so the ramp is a waste.' What is missing?
opts: Prams, trolleys, old people and anyone with a hurt leg use it too
A ramp is only for decoration
quiz.why: A ramp made for wheelchairs helps almost everyone. When we design for the person with the most difficulty, it works for many.

applications: Metro stations in Kochi, Delhi, Chennai and Bengaluru have lifts, ramps and yellow tiles. Wheelchair users, parents with prams and blind passengers can travel without help.
Many city buses in Chennai, Bengaluru and Delhi are low-floor buses with a wide, low step. Old people, people with prams and people with sticks can board more easily.
A charity in Jaipur has fitted the Jaipur Foot free of charge since 1975. The wearer can squat, climb and walk barefoot.
Many bank notes carry a raised mark. A person who cannot see can tell a hundred-rupee note from a five-hundred-rupee note by touch.
News on television often has a small window with a person signing in sign language, so that a deaf viewer can follow it. India set up a centre for Indian Sign Language in New Delhi in 2015.
Animal rescue groups in cities such as Chennai, Hyderabad and Jaipur treat hurt street dogs, cows and birds. They ask people to put out water in the hot months.

open_questions.q: Do ants, rats and fish feel anything when they are hurt or when they help?
open_questions.why_open: Their behaviour and their nerves point towards feeling. But science has no instrument that detects inner experience, even in humans. It can only compare behaviour and brains, and scientists weigh that evidence differently.

open_questions.q: Why did caring for the weak arise at all, when it costs the carer food and effort?
open_questions.why_open: Help to relatives, help that is returned, and groups that do well together have each been proposed. Each explains some cases. Care for strangers and for other species fits none of them neatly.

open_questions.q: Did the people who fed the injured man at Shanidar feel what we call compassion?
open_questions.why_open: Bones record survival and healing. They do not record feelings or reasons. Archaeologists disagree about how far it is fair to read care into them.

open_questions.q: What is the best way to teach a deaf child: sign language, an implant and speech, or both?
open_questions.why_open: Studies show that early, rich language of any kind is what matters most. But children, families and schools differ so much that no single plan has been shown to be best for all.

open_questions.q: How should a country count and pay for care work done at home?
open_questions.why_open: Economists can measure the hours. They do not agree on how to value them, or on who should pay: families, employers or the government. Countries are trying different answers.

maths.problem: A step is 10 centimetres high. A proper ramp rises 1 centimetre for every 12 centimetres along. How long must the ramp be? Your floor has only 100 centimetres of room. How much too short is it, and how could a turn help?
maths.answer: The ramp must be 120 centimetres. The floor is 20 centimetres too short. A turn splits the ramp into two runs of 60 centimetres, which each fit.
maths.explain: 10 steps of 1 centimetre up means 10 steps of 12 centimetres along. 10 x 12 = 120. 120 - 100 = 20, so the floor is 20 centimetres short. Two runs of 60 centimetres fit in a space of 100, with a flat landing at the turn.
maths.why_maths: The 1 in 12 rule is a ratio. Multiplying the height by 12 tells builders how much room a ramp needs, and shows when a turn is needed.

roots.context: You have tested a ramp and learned how to offer help. Now we ask what needing and giving help tell us about who we are.

deep_truth.truth: A step stopped the loaded cart, and a long plank let it climb with a small push. The cart did not change. So 'cannot' was never inside the cart alone. It sat between the cart and the step. People are like this too. What a person is able to do always depends on the world that meets them.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'she can't walk in' or 'he is helpless' as if being unable were a thing inside a person, like the colour of their eyes. That label makes helper and helped look like two kinds of people.
deep_truth.evidence: In the ramp test the same load needed a big stretch of the rubber band on the steep plank and a small stretch on the long plank. One and the same cart was 'unable' and 'able' within a minute, and only the plank had changed.

three.who_am_i: You have been carried, fed and taught by others every day of your life. What you can do was built by many hands. So you are not a separate self who sometimes helps. You are someone made by help, who passes it on.
three.what_is_life: No living being manages alone. A baby needs a parent, an old elephant needs the herd, a wounded ant needs a nestmate. A life is held up by other lives at its start, at its end, and at many points between.
three.what_is_this_world: A step or a ramp, a notice in one script or in two: the world we build decides who can take part in it. The world is not finished. Every doorway is a choice about who belongs, and you will help to make those choices.

roots.thread: The lesson's science is small and exact: a longer slope needs a smaller push. It carries a large idea. Ability is something that happens between a body and its surroundings. If that is so, then the line between 'the helpless' and 'the able' is drawn by how we build and behave. It also means that helping is less a gift from one separate person to another than a repair to something that joins them. Many old teachers said that the one who helps and the one helped are not truly two. Scientists who study evolution give a different account, and it is set out below.

teachings.teaching: One who sees all beings in their own self, and their own self in all beings, does not shrink away from anyone.
teachings.link: Shrinking away is what people often do on meeting someone whose body or mind is different. The verse says the cure is seeing clearly. The lesson gives one piece of that seeing: the person in the wheelchair and the person on foot differ less than the step makes it seem.

teachings.teaching: What is the use of all one's knowledge, if one does not guard another's pain as one's own?
teachings.link: The scientists who showed that trout and rats react to hurt were doing what the verse asks, with instruments. The verse adds what no instrument gives: that knowing this must change how we act.

teachings.teaching: After washing a sick monk whom the others had neglected, the Buddha said: you have no mother or father here to look after you. If you do not look after each other, who will? Whoever would look after me should look after the sick.
teachings.link: This is care given as a plain duty among equals, with no pity in it. It is close to what disabled people's groups ask for now: help that is owed.

science.text: Skeletons from tens of thousands of years ago show people surviving for years with injuries they could not have survived alone.
Whether rescue and wound care in ants, rats and elephants come with a feeling like human concern is argued over, because feeling cannot be measured from outside.

other_view.who: Biologists following William Hamilton (1964) and Richard Dawkins (1976)
other_view.view: Helping exists because, over a very long time, animals who helped their relatives and their helpful neighbours left more young than those who did not. On this view each being is separate, and care is a clever way for separate beings to do well. It needs no oneness to explain it. The warm feeling is how the habit works from inside.

practice.title: The other side of the door
practice.say: Stand at the main door of your home. Look at it as if you were someone else. First, be a person in a wheelchair. Is there a step? Is the door wide enough? Now be a person who cannot see. How would you find the bell? Now be very old and very tired. Is there somewhere to sit? Close your eyes and take three slow breaths. Think of one person you know who needs help, and of one thing they might like to be asked. Tell me what you would ask.
practice.kid: Stand at your front door. Pretend you use a wheelchair. Can you get in? Pretend you cannot see. Can you find the bell? Shut your eyes and breathe three times. Think of one person you could ask, 'Would you like some help?'

ask: When you help someone, where does the help come from: from you, or from everyone who ever helped you?
If a ramp can make a 'cannot' disappear, how many other 'cannots' might be in the building and not in the person?
Are the one who helps and the one who is helped two different kinds of people, or one kind at two different moments?
roots.art: Two hands meeting at an elbow, one old and one young, with a ramp and an open doorway in soft light behind them.

how_we_found_out.story: Before the 1800s most people believed that blind children could not be taught to read, or should read the same letters as everyone else. In 1784 Valentin Haüy opened the first school for blind children in Paris. He printed books with ordinary letters pressed up from the page. It seemed sensible, because letters were the only writing that sighted teachers knew. But raised letters are slow to tell apart by touch, the books were enormous, and a child could not write them. In 1821 a soldier named Charles Barbier brought the school a code of raised dots that he had made for passing messages at night. It used up to twelve dots, too many to feel with one touch. A pupil at the school, Louis Braille, had been blind since an accident at the age of three. He worked on the idea for three years. In 1824, aged fifteen, he had a cell of six dots that fits under one fingertip, with patterns for letters, numbers and music. The pupils took to it at once. The sighted teachers did not. One director banned it, and children were punished for using it. They used it in secret. France accepted Braille officially in 1854, two years after Louis Braille had died.
how_we_found_out.who: Valentin Haüy, Charles Barbier, Louis Braille
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed that blind readers should use raised ordinary letters. It was believable because sighted teachers judged by eye, and raised letters looked right to them, though they were poor for fingers.

playtest: Planned as a parent and child in a flat. Nothing in this lesson has been tried by a real family yet. Parts to try first: the rubber-band ramp test (the order of the three ways should always show, but the numbers depend on the band and the toy), the chappal test on a wet tray, and the dal-grain Braille names, where the glue must dry for about 20 minutes. The water dish for birds and squirrels needs two weeks, and in winter or heavy rain nobody may come. The one-hand-one-eye hook in the intro and the Hands full activity show a small difficulty for a minute and do not show what it is like to live with a disability, so tell your child that. If your child or someone at home lives with a disability, they are the expert in the room: ask them what these cards got right and wrong. Facts still to check against their sources: the World Health Organization count of 1.3 billion people and the census figures; the word divyang since 2016 and the objections to it; the 1 in 12 ramp slope in India's guidelines; the dates for Braille, Farffler, Everest and Jennings, Berkeley kerb cuts, Seiichi Miyake, Stokoe, the Milan congress and Nicaraguan Sign Language; the Jaipur Foot dates, Sudha Chandran, Arunima Sinha and Avani Lekhara; the Shanidar and Man Bac skeletons; the studies on ants, rats and vampire bats; Ashoka's Rock Edict 2, Thirukkural 315 and the other texts named; the 2012 and 2024 declarations on animal consciousness; the 2019 Time Use Survey; the last wild polio case in India in 2011; and the raised marks on the 100, 200 and 500 rupee notes. quiz: Only some people ever need help.
Everybody needs help at some time: as a baby, when ill or hurt, and often in old age.
A long ramp needs a smaller push than a short ramp for the same step.
The long ramp rises a little at a time, so the push is smaller. You push along a longer path.
A ramp should be 12 times as long as the step is high or longer.
India's guidelines say a wheelchair ramp should rise no more than 1 centimetre for every 12 along.
Braille is read with the ears.
Braille is raised dots that fingertips read.
You should ask first before helping a person.
Asking lets the person stay in charge of their own body and choices.
Indian Sign Language is the same as American Sign Language.
Each country has its own sign languages, as it has its own spoken languages.
A rough mat grips better than a smooth wet floor.
A rough surface lets feet, sticks and wheels grip even when it is wet.
Old people have nothing to teach young people.
Old people carry recipes, songs, cures and stories that are written in no book.
A wagging tail always means a dog is happy to see you.
A tail can wag when a dog is excited or worried. Watch her whole body, such as her ears, her face and how she stands.
Help is only a favour from kind people.
Help to enter a school or catch a bus is a right. A step that is in the way should go.
odd: The first three are aids that help with seeing or hearing. A skipping rope is a toy.
The first, second and fourth stop people from getting in. A ramp opens the way.
Rest, water and company help a sick person. Loud noise does not.
The first three are animals who may need water. A wall is not alive.
The others can be used with an elbow or a hand that cannot grip. A round knob needs a hand that can grip and turn.
